text: Eigenvectors told us which directions a matrix leaves on their own line, but some matrices have none, and a rectangular matrix, which turns a list of one length into a list of another, cannot have them at all. The singular value decomposition makes a promise that holds for every matrix: it is a rotation, then a stretch along the axes, then another rotation.

Watch what a matrix does to a circle of arrows of length one. The circle always becomes an ellipse. The longest axis of that ellipse is the direction the matrix stretches most, and its half length is the first singular value; the shortest axis gives the second singular value, and the two axes always meet at a right angle.

Now play the transformation in three moves. First, a rotation called V transpose turns the special input directions onto the axes. Then a diagonal matrix, sigma, stretches along those axes by the singular values. Finally, a rotation called U turns the result into place. Any matrix, however much it shears and skews the plane, is exactly these simple motions one after another, where a rotation may also include a mirror flip.

The singular values come sorted from largest to smallest, and that order tells you what matters. If one is large and the other tiny, the matrix squeezes the plane almost onto a line, so keeping only the largest part gives an approximation that is nearly as good as the original while storing far fewer numbers. This is a low rank approximation, and a theorem of Eckart and Young says that keeping the top singular values gives the best one possible.

Principal component analysis puts this to work on data. Imagine a cloud of points, such as people measured by height and weight, that lies along a slanted band shaped like a cigar. First subtract the average so the cloud is centred on the origin, then take the singular value decomposition of the data. The first right singular vector points along the length of the cigar, the direction of greatest spread, and it is called the first principal component.

Projecting each point onto that direction, the shadow from the lesson on dot products, turns two numbers per person into one, and very little is lost, because the cloud was thin in the other direction anyway. With hundreds of dimensions, the same move keeps the few directions that carry most of the variation and drops the rest, which is how people draw flat maps of word embeddings.

The same idea sits behind LoRA, a popular way to fine tune a large language model cheaply. Instead of updating a huge weight matrix, it learns a low rank update, the product of two thin matrices, betting that the change a new task needs lives in only a few directions. That completes our linear algebra toolkit. Next we begin calculus, with the derivative as the slope of a curve seen under a microscope.
